title: Wave Phenomena
summary: ## Waves
A wave is a disturbance that carries energy, not matter, from one place to another.

Transverse waves: particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel, as in waves on a string, ripples on water and light. Longitudinal waves: particles vibrate along the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions, as in sound. Sound is longitudinal, so it cannot be polarized.
## Wave terms
Wavelength λ, frequency ν, period T = 1/ν and speed v = νλ. When a wave enters a new medium its frequency stays the same, so λ changes in proportion to v: if the speed doubles, λ doubles.
Phase difference = (2π/λ) × path difference.

A progressive wave is y = A sin(ωt − kx), with ω = 2πν and k = 2π/λ. Particle velocity ∂y/∂t = Aω cos(ωt − kx) leads the displacement by π/2; its maximum is Aω. Example: y = 3 sin(36t + 0.018x) has ω = 36 rad/s, so T ≈ 0.17 s, and k = 0.018 /m, so λ ≈ 349 m; it moves along −x.
Example: waves with crests 100 m apart moving at 25 m/s rock a boat every T = λ/v = 4 s.
## Speed of waves
On a string: v = √(T/μ), where T is the tension and μ the mass per unit length.

Sound in a gas: Newton took v = √(P/ρ) (isothermal), which gives about 280 m/s, too low. Laplace corrected it because the compressions and rarefactions are so rapid that the process is adiabatic: v = √(γP/ρ) ≈ 332 m/s at 0 °C.

The speed of sound is proportional to √T, rising by about 0.61 m/s per °C. It is unaffected by pressure at constant temperature, increases with humidity (moist air is less dense), and is greatest in solids, then liquids, then gases.
## Superposition, beats and stationary waves
Beats: two sounds of nearly equal frequencies ν₁ and ν₂ give ν₁ − ν₂ beats per second. Beats are used to find an unknown frequency; loading a fork with wax lowers its frequency.

Stationary waves form when two identical waves travel in opposite directions, y = 2A sin kx cos ωt. Nodes and antinodes are λ/2 apart, and a node is λ/4 from the next antinode. Stationary waves transfer no energy.
A sonometer wire carries transverse stationary waves, and a resonance column carries longitudinal ones. Resonance is a case of forced vibration.
## Organ pipes
Open pipe: fundamental ν = v/2L, with all harmonics present.
Closed pipe: fundamental ν = v/4L, with only odd harmonics; the second harmonic is missing. For equal lengths, ν_open : ν_closed = 2 : 1, and pipes in unison need L_open = 2L_closed.
Overtones are the frequencies above the fundamental. In a closed pipe the first overtone is the 3rd harmonic, so all harmonics are overtones but not all overtones are harmonics.
## Characteristics of musical sound

Pitch depends on frequency, loudness on intensity (the square of the amplitude), and quality (timbre) on the overtones present. Pitch is a sensation and frequency a physical quantity; the same holds for loudness and intensity. An intensity ratio of 1 : 16 means an amplitude ratio of 1 : 4.
## Doppler effect

The apparent frequency changes when the source or observer moves. For a source approaching a stationary observer, ν' = νv/(v − vₛ), and the wavelength becomes λ' = (v − vₛ)/ν. For a receding source, ν' = νv/(v + vₛ). Applications include radar, police speed guns, measuring stars' speeds (red shift) and SONAR, which uses ultrasonic waves.
## Electromagnetic spectrum

In order of increasing frequency: radio waves, microwaves, infrared ('heat waves'), visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Gamma rays have wavelengths shorter than X-rays and are the most energetic.

vsa: Name the factors on which the speed of a wave on a stretched string depends.
v = √(T/μ): it depends on the tension T in the string and its mass per unit length μ. More tension gives higher speed; a heavier string gives lower speed.
October 2025
'All harmonics are overtones but all overtones are not harmonics.' Explain.

Harmonics are integral multiples of the fundamental. Overtones are the frequencies actually produced above the fundamental. In a closed pipe only odd harmonics occur, so the first overtone is the 3rd harmonic and the 2nd harmonic is missing. Every overtone is a harmonic, but not every harmonic appears as an overtone.
October 2025
Distinguish between (i) pitch and frequency and (ii) loudness and intensity.

(i) Frequency is the number of vibrations per second (a physical quantity); pitch is the sensation of shrillness, which depends on frequency.
(ii) Intensity is the energy flowing per second per unit area (∝ amplitude²); loudness is the ear's sensation of it.
October 2024
Give two differences between stationary and travelling waves.

(1) A travelling wave transfers energy; a stationary wave does not.
(2) In a travelling wave every particle has the same amplitude; in a stationary wave the amplitude varies from zero at nodes to maximum at antinodes.

An open pipe of length l₁ and a closed pipe of length l₂ resonate with the same fork in their fundamental modes. Find l₁/l₂.

Give two differences between transverse and longitudinal waves.

(1) In transverse waves particles vibrate perpendicular to the wave direction; in longitudinal waves, along it.
(2) Transverse waves form crests and troughs; longitudinal waves form compressions and rarefactions. Transverse waves can be polarized; longitudinal waves cannot.

sa: A source of sound of frequency 1 kHz moves towards a stationary observer at 40 m/s. Find the wavelength received when (i) both are at rest and (ii) the source moves. (v = 340 m/s)

(i) λ = v/ν = 340/1000 = 0.34 m.
(ii) The waves are crowded together: λ' = (v − vₛ)/ν = (340 − 40)/1000 = 0.30 m.
The apparent frequency is 340/0.30 ≈ 1133 Hz.
Write Newton's formula for the speed of sound in air. Why and how did Laplace correct it?

Newton assumed isothermal changes: v = √(P/ρ) ≈ 280 m/s at NTP, much less than the measured 332 m/s.
Laplace pointed out that compressions and rarefactions are so rapid, and air such a poor conductor, that the process is adiabatic. Then the elasticity is γP, so v = √(γP/ρ) = √(1.4 × 1.013 × 10⁵/1.29) ≈ 332 m/s, agreeing with experiment.
How is the speed of sound in air affected by temperature, pressure, density and humidity? At what temperature does it become twice its value at 27 °C?

Temperature: v ∝ √T, so it rises with temperature. Pressure: no effect at constant temperature (P/ρ stays constant). Density: v ∝ 1/√ρ. Humidity: moist air is less dense, so v increases.
For v to double, T must be 4 times: 4 × 300 = 1200 K = 927 °C.
What are beats? How are they used to find the unknown frequency of a tuning fork?

Beats are the periodic rise and fall of loudness when two sounds of slightly different frequencies are heard together. The number of beats per second = ν₁ − ν₂.
Sound the unknown fork with a known fork (ν) and count the beats b: the unknown is ν ± b. Load the unknown fork with wax (lowering its frequency): if the beats increase, it was ν − b; if they decrease, it was ν + b.
la: State the Doppler effect. A source emits 5 kHz. Find the frequency received when (i) source and observer are at rest, (ii) the source approaches a stationary observer at 30 m/s, (iii) it recedes at 30 m/s. (v = 330 m/s) Give two applications.

Doppler effect: the apparent change in frequency of a wave due to relative motion of the source and the observer.
(i) ν = 5000 Hz.
(ii) ν' = νv/(v − vₛ) = 5000 × 330/300 = 5500 Hz.
(iii) ν' = νv/(v + vₛ) = 5000 × 330/360 ≈ 4583 Hz.
Applications: radar and police speed guns; finding the speed of stars from red shift; SONAR; medical ultrasound (blood-flow measurement).
Derive the equation of a plane progressive harmonic wave. Show that the particle velocity leads the displacement by π/2.

The source vibrates as y = A sin ωt. A particle at distance x starts x/v later, so y = A sin ω(t − x/v) = A sin(ωt − kx), with k = ω/v = 2π/λ.
Particle velocity u = ∂y/∂t = Aω cos(ωt − kx) = Aω sin(ωt − kx + π/2).
So the velocity leads the displacement by π/2, and its maximum value is Aω.
Explain the formation of stationary waves in an air column. Show that an open pipe gives all harmonics but a closed pipe gives only odd harmonics.

When a wave is reflected back on itself, the incident and reflected waves superpose to form a stationary wave, y = 2A sin kx cos ωt, with fixed nodes and antinodes λ/2 apart.
Closed pipe: a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4 …, giving ν = v/4L, 3v/4L, 5v/4L — only odd harmonics.
Open pipe: antinodes at both ends, so L = λ/2, λ, 3λ/2 …, giving ν = v/2L, 2v/2L, 3v/2L — all harmonics.
So an open pipe's fundamental is twice that of a closed pipe of the same length.
